flags.text: JAR is Java ARchive and the coffee-cup mark applies, so this is the flag to argue with if any of them is. Why it is not shipped: (1) sourcing — Oracle publishes no Java mark under citable terms and simple-icons has no java entry in v16.29.0, so both of L2's first two tiers are empty; the only faithful vector available is vscode-icons' trace. (2) legibility — the mark it traces is a calligraphic drawing of eight tapering brush strokes with no solid cup anywhere in it. Every stroke is sub-pixel at 16 px, and the only reduction that would read is a redrawn cup, which is freehand geometry for a brand that owns a mark: L2's hard reject, and the exact failure that got round 1 thrown out. So jar takes the archive box, byte-identical with vsix. To overturn this you would have to rule twice — once that a third-party trace of an Oracle mark is an acceptable source, and once that redrawing it is an acceptable reduction.

flags.title: chrome — Google's own SVG, four official colours, and a 0.64 px white ring
flags.text: Google publishes chrome-logo.svg on google.com/chrome, so the brand tier wins outright over simple-icons' monochrome silhouette and R1 keeps all four colours. Two things to look at. The gradients: the three blades are painted with linear gradients and L2 flattens each to its dominant flat stop — the offset-1 stop of each, which lands exactly on Google's published flat palette (#EA4335 / #FBBC04 / #34A853). The white ring: the official separator between the blue centre (r 9.5) and the blades (r 12) is 2.5/48 of the mark, which is 0.64 px at this envelope. It is kept at official proportions and renders as a light seam rather than a ring — the same reading L5's erratum already applied to docker's 0.28 px container gaps and editorconfig's 0.2 px linework. Thickening it to clear 1.2 px means shrinking Google's blue centre from r 9.5 to r 7.5 — a fifth off its diameter. Kept faithful; say the word and it thickens. Licence, honestly: no declared terms, Google trademark — the editorconfig situation again.

flags.title: onnx — the prettier rider thickens a wireframe without moving it
flags.text: The ONNX icon IS its edges: a heptagonal outline with eight triangular facets knocked out, and measured at the shipped fit those edges are 0.35 px. Unreadable as published, so the rider fires. The reduction is mechanical rather than editorial: each facet counter is scaled about its own bbox centre by 0.8, which takes the internal edges to 0.50–0.84 px and leaves the outline, the vertex positions, the facet count and every angle exactly where the official file puts them. Nothing is deleted, nothing is redrawn — the facets shrink, the drawing does not move. And it does not clear L5, which you should know before ruling: after the shrink the narrowest place is the rim where a facet corner meets one of the outline's rounded vertex nodes, and that rim sits at 0.36 px however far the facets go. It renders as antialiasing, exactly as editorconfig's 0.2 px linework does. Deleting facets to buy thick ink was measured — 4 and 5 of the 8 kept, at three shrink factors, all in proofs/onnx-edge-study.png — and rejected: it turns the polyhedron into a blob with slits and stops being the mark. The honest 16 px verdict is marginal, and the alternatives are worse. Colour: ONNX's own icon file is achromatic (seven gray/white facets over #333333 edges); #005CED is the brand blue the CC0 trace records and what ships, because an achromatic ONNX would sit in the neutral lane next to the mark-less glyphs. Licence: the brand's own file is kept in sources-svg/ for the fidelity strip but does not ship — onnx/onnx.github.io declares no licence, so the CC0 trace of the same drawing is what the geometry comes from.

flags.title: safetensors is NOT stamped with the Hugging Face face
flags.superseded: SUPERSEDED by the fix-round ruling (2026-09-03) — the real-icon preference overturns the decline and the HF face ships. The MEANING objection this flag makes is a different question from the licence ones the ruling settles, so it is carried forward for a re-look rather than dismissed: see flag 38.
flags.text: The brief asked the question, so here is the answer with the evidence. The format is Hugging Face's — github.com/huggingface/safetensors — and HF does publish an official vector of its mark. It is deliberately not used: safetensors publishes no mark of its OWN, and HF's smiling face is the company's mark, not the format's. .safetensors files are written by dozens of tools with no Hugging Face connection, so stamping the face on all of them claims an ownership the format does not carry — unlike .pt (PyTorch's own format, PyTorch's own mark) or .onnx, where the project and the format are the same thing. It is not a rule-1 family variant either. vscode-icons independently draws a neutral glyph. Overturn it and safetensors becomes the HF face; the artwork is one fetch away.

flags.title: android, gpg and onnx ship from simple-icons after the brand tier came up empty
flags.text: L2 asks for the brand's own vector first, and the hunt is recorded rather than assumed. android: developer.android.com and android.com publish the robot as PNG only (Android_Robot_100.png answers 200; every SVG path answers 404), and tracing a PNG is freehand. gpg: GnuPG's artwork lives in the project's git tree at git.gnupg.org, which answered 429 Too Many Requests / GnuPG Git Maintenance on every attempt; gnupg.org itself ships the logo as PNG. onnx: the brand's file was fetched and is in sources-svg/, but its repo declares no licence. All three therefore ship from simple-icons' CC0 traces, which is L2's second tier working exactly as written. If any of the three matters enough, the brand file can be re-hunted later without touching the geometry pipeline.

flags.title: debian keeps the swirl and drops eleven brush flecks
flags.text: The Open Use Logo is an Illustrator export of a brush drawing: one long path for the spiral and eleven detached specks for the flecks the brush left. At this fit the specks measure 0.02–0.63 px in their minor axis, every one of them under two thirds of a pixel, so L5 drops them; the spiral is the official path with nothing changed. What you should judge at 16 px is the spiral's own taper — the brush thins to nothing at the tail by construction, the way yaml's letters are thin by construction. That is the mark, not the fit.

flags.title: gpg is repainted two-colour from a single-path trace
flags.text: The official GnuPG logo is a blue padlock with the GNU's mane printed WHITE across it. simple-icons, like all its icons, is single-path, so the trace knocks the mane out as a counter and it would render as backdrop-through-lock. R1 keeps multi-colour marks multi-colour, so the mane subpath is painted #FFFFFF over the lock instead of being left as a hole — the same move the pilot made on typescript's S and T. No geometry changes: same three subpaths, same winding, official colours. The shackle's opening stays a counter, as the mark draws it.

flags.title: angular — seven ids, ONE payload, and Material's seven colours are Material's
flags.text: The brief expected these to be rule 1(a) — adapt Material's established variant glyphs in Angular's colours. Material has no variant glyphs. Its own file-icon definitions declare every one of the seven as clone: { base: "angular", color: <material palette name> }: the base mark recoloured and nothing else, with no angular-component.svg or its kin anywhere in the theme. vscode-icons and Great Icons draw no angular variants at all. So branch (a) has nothing to adapt and branch (b) fires: all seven ship the Angular mark byte-identically, in Angular's own #DD0031 from brand-colors.json, and the check asserts that identity rather than trusting it. The alternative, measured: adopt Material's hues — #1976D2, #BA68C8, #43A047, #FB8C00, #00897B, #43A047, #FFCA28. They are invented by Material for Material, R1 has no place for invented colour, and they do not even separate the seven: guard and resolver get the SAME green, so seven concepts come out in six colours. All eight candidates are rendered at a true 16 px in proofs/angular-variants-study.png. What you are ruling on: in the tree a user.component.ts, a auth.guard.ts and a api.service.ts will all show the same red Angular A. Say the word and they become seven hues that no brand publishes. Which mark: the 2023 A, not the 2016 red shield — angular.dev/press-kit deprecates the shield outright. Which red: the 2023 mark is published as a gradient plus flat black and white, and as PNG/GIF only, with no SVG anywhere in the press kit; brand-colors wins the primary hex by the pilot's own ruling, so #DD0031 it is.

flags.title: RULE 2 at scale — twelve of thirty-five collapse onto one glyph
flags.superseded: PARTLY SUPERSEDED by the fix-round ruling (2026-09-03). SEVEN of the thirteen left the pile: the six corporate marks (actionscript, adobe-swc, al, al-dal, apex, applescript) ship their real marks, and antlr is reinstated under a declared look-alike lane. SIX remain — ada, affectscript, agda, ahk2, anyscript, apl — and every one of those is a legibility or a no-mark-at-all verdict, not a licence one. See flags 40, 41 and 42.
flags.text: This is the biggest single fact about the tranche and it should not arrive as a surprise on the sheet. Thirteen of thirty-five concepts ship the generic-code category glyph, byte for byte, so thirteen rows of the file tree will carry the same gray angle brackets. They fall into four different piles and the flags below take them separately: six are corporate marks this build DECLINES (actionscript, adobe-swc, al, al-dal, apex, applescript), four are real marks that CANNOT SURVIVE 16 px (ada, agda, ahk2, apl), one was built from its mark and then FAILED BY THE TWIN AUDIT (antlr), and two own no mark at all (affectscript, anyscript). Overturning any one flag moves subjects out of the pile. The glyph itself is tranche 1's generic-code, used here for the first time; it is placed at 1.16x its authored size so twelve shared rows carry the set's normal ink mass (148) instead of 110 — the same move tranche 1 made on generic-binary. abc is NOT in this pile: .abc is music notation, so it gets an object glyph (a note, new in geom.mjs) the way disc and lib did.

flags.title: Six corporate marks declined — and the line this tranche drew, stated so you can move it
flags.superseded: SUPERSEDED IN FULL by the fix-round ruling (2026-09-03). This flag's own closing sentence named the lever — "to overturn: rule that a theme's MIT-licensed trace of a removed corporate mark is an acceptable source, and six icons change in one edit" — and that is exactly what happened. All six ship their real marks; see flag 40. Kept in place because the hunts it records are still the hunts, and because its Microsoft half was already corrected by flag 25.
flags.text: Tranche 1 declined the VS Code ribbon and the Java cup. This tranche had six more of the same shape and applied one testable rule rather than six judgement calls. The rule: for a brand this large, ABSENCE from simple-icons is evidence of a trademark removal, not of obscurity — a CC0 library carrying 3,457 brands does not simply forget Adobe. Where both L2 tiers are empty (no brand vector under citable terms AND no CC0 trace) the mark is declined. Adobe (actionscript, adobe-swc): no Adobe marks remain in v16.29.0, same removal that took Microsoft's. Microsoft (al, al-dal): tranche 1's vsix finding, unchanged, plus this set ships inside a VS Code fork. Salesforce (apex): no salesforce entry, no citable vector — and this is the painful one, because the Salesforce cloud is a clean silhouette that would have rendered beautifully at 16 px. It is declined on sourcing alone. Apple (applescript) is the exception that proves the rule is not mechanical: simple-icons DOES carry apple (CC0), so the tier is not empty — it is declined because the Apple logo is the COMPANY's mark and not AppleScript's (tranche 1's safetensors reading) and because Apple's identity guidelines forbid third-party use outright. Both Material and vscode-icons desaturate it, which is a tell. The counter-example is abap: SAP IS in simple-icons, so ABAP ships the SAP mark. That is what makes the line a line and not a mood. To overturn: rule that a theme's MIT-licensed trace of a removed corporate mark is an acceptable source, and six icons change in one edit.

flags.title: Four marks that exist, are published, and cannot hold 16 px
flags.superseded: RE-TESTED, NOT SUPERSEDED (fix round, 2026-09-03). Sourcing is free now, so all four were re-measured with the whole pool open and every one still fails on L5 — the ruling freed the licences, not the physics. ONE FACTUAL CORRECTION: this flag says of ahk2 that #334455 at 1.86:1 is a contrast the lift rule cannot reach "above the L 22 trigger". The fix round re-derived that trigger to test CONTRAST at 3.0:1 rather than lightness, so the rule does reach it now — and it changes nothing, because this flag's own study already rendered the mark lifted and it is exactly as illegible. The new measurements and every reduction attempted are in flag 42.
flags.text: These are NOT sourcing declines — the artwork is real and two of them are cleanly licensed. They are legibility declines, and proofs/agda-and-friends-study.png renders every candidate at a true 16 px so the verdicts can be checked instead of believed. agda: the project's own bird (agda/agda, doc/user-manual/agda.svg) is drawn ENTIRELY in strokes — 36 units on a 1200-unit mark, i.e. 0.37 px — and L8 bans strokes. Thicken to L5's 1.2 px floor and the three parallel head strokes, which have 0.73 px of clearance, fuse into one wedge; thicken further and it is a blot. Its body outline is open, so it cannot be filled as a silhouette without inventing the closure. ada: ada-lang.io's mark is a three-letter LOGOTYPE (simple-icons ada, CC0). At the flat envelope — the widest fit the grid allows — the whole thing is 15.2 × 6.5 px and its ink runs measure 0.50–1.00 px. This is the npm-wordmark case the pilot already ruled on, except Ada publishes no square mark to fall back to. ahk2: AutoHotkey's keycap has nothing in it over 0.50 px of sustained ink, and its official #334455 measures 1.86:1 against the editor ground — no lift rule reaches it (L 26.7, above the L 22 trigger) and inventing a brighter AutoHotkey blue is not R1's to do. apl: APL has no owner, so there is no official mark at all; the APL Wiki's community logo is an apple-cube whose defining feature is a matrix subdivision, and aplwiki.com refuses automated fetches (403 on every attempt). To overturn any of these you are ruling that an icon may ship illegible, which is the one thing every version of this style guide has refused.

flags.title: abap ships the SAP mark — letters and all
flags.text: The corporate-mark flag needs a counter-example or it is just a mood, and this is it. ABAP is SAP's language and .abap files exist nowhere but inside a SAP system, so the SAP mark applies (the AdvPL reading, and the opposite of tranche 1's safetensors call). SAP publishes its own vector AND simple-icons carries a CC0 trace, so unlike Adobe and Microsoft neither tier is empty. The geometry is the CC0 trace, not SAP's own file, for a boring reason: SAP's file paints its field with a <polyline>, which is not a path, and rebuilding it would mean transcribing brand coordinates by hand. The brand file is fetched to sources-svg/sap-official.svg and is what the fidelity strip shows. What to look at: the letters. Measured on the shipped 16 px render, the "SAP" stems are 1.00–1.25 px — AT L5's official-forced floor rather than under it — and printed white on the mark's own blue field, which is the highest-contrast pairing in the tranche. They resolve. dotenv needed the prettier rider at 0.50 px; this does not, and no reduction was made. Licence, honestly: SAP trademark, no declared terms on the brand file; the shipped geometry is CC0.

flags.title: advpl — the BRAND draws the variants, so working rule 1 needs a third mode
flags.text: Rule 1 as written has two branches: adapt a source theme's variant glyph (a), or ship the family base identically (b). AdvPL fits neither, and it fits neither for the best possible reason. TOTVS ships the variant artwork itself. github.com/totvs/advpl-vscode — TOTVS's own VS Code extension, MIT — carries icon_advpl.svg, icon_include.svg, icon_ptm.svg and icon_tlpp.svg: the TOTVS symbol in four colours, one per file type, differing in nothing but the fill (diffed, and the geometry is character-for-character identical). So the per-variant colours here are OFFICIAL, which is exactly what Material's angular hues are not. Each variant reads its own file and ships its own hex: #337AB7 blue, #33B7B6 teal, #B73733 red, #B7AC33 olive. The declaration: the family is recorded with mode: "recolour", byte-identity is NOT expected, and the twin audit prints the four in its family lane with their real form scores instead of failing them for sharing a silhouette. If you would rather rule 1 stayed a two-branch rule, the alternative is collapsing all four onto one blue icon under branch (b) — which would throw away colour the brand publishes.

flags.title: affinity and affinitypublisher — one live mark, one retired one
flags.text: Two calls in one subject pair. The mark: Serif/Canva serves the Affinity mark as a plain SVG at affinity.serif.com/favicon.svg — the pale-green field with the black "a" swirl — so the brand tier wins outright and vscode-icons traces the same drawing. Licence: none declared, Serif/Canva trademark. That is the chrome situation from tranche 1 and it is flagged the same way. The family: .afpub is an Affinity Publisher document, and Publisher DID have its own app icon in the Affinity 2 suite — the red "canyon" illustration vscode-icons still traces. Serif/Canva retired the three per-app icons when Affinity became one application, so the mark the brand publishes for .afpub today is the Affinity mark itself; and the retired icon would not have survived anyway, being an eleven-layer gradient illustration that R1 flattens to a red triangle — the exact gestalt failure the pilot gate rejected on docker and editorconfig. So rule 1(b): affinitypublisher ships the Affinity mark byte-identically. To overturn: rule that a retired app icon is still the file type's mark, and accept the flattening.

flags.title: antlr — sourced, built, and then removed by the twin audit
flags.superseded: SUPERSEDED by the fix-round ruling (2026-09-03) — this flag's SECOND option was taken: "rule that two brands whose real marks genuinely resemble each other may both keep them and relax R8 for declared pairs". antlr is reinstated and the antlr/chrome pair now sits in a declared LOOK-ALIKE lane that reports these same scores every run and never fails. See flag 41 — and look at the study before you accept it.
flags.text: The one subject in this tranche whose verdict was decided by a GATE and not by a hunt, so the whole sequence is on the record. The hunt succeeded, on L2's third tier — the first time that tier has fired anywhere in this set. antlr.org publishes the mark (an orange-red disc with a white "A") only as images/antlr-logo.png, 220 × 80; every SVG path on the site and in antlr/website-antlr4 answers 404, and tracing a PNG is freehand. simple-icons has no antlr entry — NOT the Adobe situation, just a small BSD-licensed project. Three independent faithful vectors of the same drawing exist (vscode-icons MIT, Material MIT, mike-lischke/vscode-antlr4) and vscode-icons' carries the disc AND the "A" in the mark's own two-layer construction. It was built from that vector and its 16 px render was the cleanest circle-and-glyph in the slice. Then the cross-set twin audit failed it against tranche 1's chrome: R8 form 0.798 against the 0.72 bar (area IoU 0.969 — two discs of the same diameter are one silhouette), and R7 on top of it, ANTLR's #E44A32 and Chrome's #EA4335 being 3.4 degrees of hue apart. In the tree a .crx and a .g4 would have been the same red disc. No fit fixes it: the envelope law has no room to shrink one disc by a quarter. Both renders are side by side at a true 16 px in proofs/antlr-chrome-study.png. Your options: accept the neutral glyph (what ships); rule that two brands whose real marks genuinely resemble each other may both keep them and relax R8 for declared pairs; or re-treat chrome, which is tranche 1's and untouched here. The vector and the brand's PNG are both kept in sources-svg/, so reinstating it is a five-line edit.

flags.title: Two prettier riders, both mechanical: alchemy and apib
flags.text: Both marks are line drawings whose lines are under the floor, and both were fixed by moving nothing — the onnx principle. alchemy (circle, inscribed triangle, dot) is drawn with 1.4-unit STROKES, which L8 bans and which measure 0.90 px anyway. The stroke-to-fill conversion is exact rather than a redraw: a stroke of width t around radius r IS the annulus r ± t/2, and offsetting a triangle's three edges by t/2 produces a similar triangle about its incentre, so every vertex and angle stays put. t is then raised 1.4 → 2.0 units, landing the line on 1.23 px. apib (three rings joined by two bars) has 0.59 px ring walls and 0.44 px connectors. Each ring's counter is scaled about its own centre by 0.60 — wall 0.59 → 1.26 px, hole still 2.01 px across, outer circles and centres untouched — and the two connectors are re-emitted as 3.6-unit bars (1.21 px) between the official ring centres, which is precisely what prettier's surviving rows did. The choice worth knowing about: filling the apib rings SOLID was the easy reduction and is what Material does. It clears the floor trivially and makes it a different mark; the rings are kept as rings.

flags.title: Four brand files, no declared licences — the chrome situation, four more times
flags.superseded: SUPERSEDED as a question by the fix-round ruling (2026-09-03): licence exposure no longer needs a decision, because it no longer gates anything. The RECORD stands and grows — every source and licence is still written down verbatim, here and on every subject the fix round added.
flags.text: Tranche 1 shipped Google's chrome-logo.svg with "no declared licence — Google trademark" written on the sheet, and that precedent is now carrying weight. Four more subjects sit in the same place and each one is recorded, not smoothed over. affinity / affinitypublisher: Serif/Canva's own favicon.svg, no terms. alloy: grafana.com's own media asset, no terms — though the project it belongs to (grafana/alloy) is Apache-2.0. allure: allurereport.org's own site asset, no terms — the projects (allure2, allure3) are Apache-2.0. (antlr would have been a fourth; the twin audit removed it first.) Against that, the cleanly-licensed half of the tranche: advpl ×4 (MIT), abelljs (MIT), apib (MIT), alchemy (Apache-2.0) and everything from simple-icons (CC0). Nothing here needs a decision to proceed — it needs you to know the shape of the exposure, and to say if the bar should be higher than chrome set it.

flags.title: ahk2 has no family declared, and tranche 3 needs to know why
flags.superseded: RE-TESTED, NOT SUPERSEDED (fix round, 2026-09-03). The legibility call it rests on was re-measured from both sides and holds, so ahk2 and autohotkey both stay on the glyph and no family is declared — exactly as this flag predicted. See flag 42.
flags.text: The brief asked for a family declaration with autohotkey as a base marked pending-tranche-3, so tranche 3 could assert byte-identity from the other side. That declaration is deliberately NOT made, because the hunt came out the other way: the AutoHotkey mark cannot hold 16 px (see the legibility flag), so ahk2 ships the neutral glyph and there is no family mark for a base to be identical TO. Declaring one would have been a fiction the check would have happily passed. What tranche 3 should do: measure autohotkey itself — it is the same keycap, so the same numbers apply (nothing over 0.50 px of sustained ink, #334455 at 1.86:1) — and reach the same verdict, at which point both ids sit in the generic-code collapse and no family is needed at all. If you overturn the legibility call, ahk2 and autohotkey become a rule-1(b) family and the declaration goes in tranche 3's module, where the base actually lives.

flags.title: TOOLING — the slice sheet still describes tranche 1 only
flags.text: Not an icon call, but the sheet is what this gate is decided on, so it should not mislead. tools/build-slice-sheet.mjs hard-codes tranche 1's narrative: its header says the revision "covers the roster's archive and binary categories" (it now covers code as well), its second panel says one subject needed the prettier rider (three do), and section 5 tells you to look at "flags 3, 4 and 7", which are tranche 1's numbers. This tranche did not touch that file, on the brief's instruction that its entire integration is A01.t2.mjs. The fix is one small edit — drive those three sentences off the manifest the way the rest of the page already is — and it wants doing before tranche 3 lands and makes it worse.

flags.title: RULE 2 at slice scale — FORTY of the eighty-four are one payload
flags.superseded: SUPERSEDED by the fix-round ruling (2026-09-03). Forty is now TWENTY. This flag named both levers and the ruling pulled both: L2 (twelve subjects across the slice found real marks once licence stopped gating) and the vocabulary (the stopwatch and the terminal opened, taking five more). The pile it describes is gone; what is left is flag 49's twenty, and every one of those is a legibility verdict or a genuine absence.
flags.text: Tranche 2 flagged thirteen of thirty-five on the generic-code glyph. This tranche adds twenty-seven of thirty-six, which makes forty of the slice's eighty-four icons the same gray angle brackets, byte for byte. That is the single biggest fact about A01 and it should be the first thing you rule on, ahead of any individual mark. They are not one pile and the flags below take them separately: two are declined on a LICENCE Microsoft publishes and this build cannot meet (azure, azurestreamanalytics); five are marks that EXIST, four of them cleanly licensed, and cannot hold 16 px (appscript, aspx, autohotkey, behat, blade); four are cases where a product's or a company's mark is not the format's (bashly-hook, biml, blink, bolt); and sixteen own no artwork at all. The lever that would move the most icons at once is not any of those — it is the vocabulary. Opening three more object glyphs (a stopwatch for the bench family, a terminal for awk/bat/bashly-hook, a citation mark for the BibTeX family) would take seven concepts out of the collapse in one edit. All three are built and measured in proofs/object-glyph-study.png, and one of the three is already ruled out by R8 rather than by taste. The alternative lever is L2: rule that a source theme's MIT-licensed trace of a mark whose owner publishes no usable vector is an acceptable source, and appscript, blade and behat stop being about licensing — though all three would still be about legibility, which is flag 27.

flags.title: bench-js / -jsx / -ts — the per-language variant family, and the precedent it sets
flags.superseded: SUPERSEDED IN PART by the fix-round ruling (2026-09-03) — reading 2 SHIPS. This flag put the gray stopwatch one rule away from shipping and said so; the fix round widens that rule and takes it. Reading 3 (the languages' own hexes) is UNCHANGED and still out, for the unchanged reason. See flag 48.
flags.text: This is the smallest set of icons in the tranche and the one whose ruling travels furthest: every per-language variant family in every later slice — test-js, spec-ts, stories-tsx and their kin — lands wherever this one does. The facts. Nothing owns the *.bench.* convention; there is no bench brand. Material draws ONE stopwatch and recolours it three times in #FFCA28, #00BCD4 and #0288D1 — Material palette entries, and note that they are not JavaScript's own #F7DF1E or TypeScript's own #3178C6. vscode-icons and Great Icons draw no bench icons at all. v1 drew one stopwatch in three tints of its own. The three readings are all built and rendered at a true 16 px in proofs/bench-family-study.png. (1) the generic-code glyph — what ships. (2) one GRAY stopwatch shared by all three. (3) the stopwatch in the LANGUAGES' official hexes. Reading 3 is out on R1's own terms: it paints js's and ts's real colours onto a stopwatch neither language draws, which composes a mark no brand publishes — and using the languages' genuine hexes makes that composite more convincing, not less. Reading 2 is close, and the numbers favour it: the stopwatch clears L5 comfortably (1.38 px minimum, 2.25 px at the 25th percentile) and it is R8-clean against the entire existing vocabulary — its worst form score against disc, book, archive, binary and code is under 0.40 on a 0.72 bar. Nothing technical stands in its way. It is declined on the rule, not the numbers: working rule 2 gives a concept an object glyph where it NAMES an object — disc names a disc, lib a volume, abc a note — and a benchmark names a measurement. A stopwatch is the metaphor for a category, which is what the category glyph is for. Shipping it also opens the branch for every timing, testing and tooling concept in the long tail on identical logic. Say the word and it is one line, in this module and in every slice after it.

flags.title: CORRECTION to flag 13 — simple-icons DOES carry Microsoft marks, and .NET is CC0
flags.text: Tranche 2's corporate-mark flag rests on a testable claim — "for a brand this large, ABSENCE from simple-icons is evidence of a trademark removal" — and it states that no Microsoft marks remain in v16.29.0. That part is not correct, and this tranche checked it because aspx made it load-bearing. v16.29.0 carries dotnet (#512BD4) and blazor, and it records dotnet's source as github.com/dotnet/brand/logo/dotnet-logo.svg with a declared CC0-1.0 licence. That repository is Microsoft's own .NET brand repo; it is licensed CC0-1.0 and its README says you may "use the illustrations and logo to represent .NET in related content". The file is fetched to sources-svg/dotnet-official.svg. What this changes: the ADOBE, SALESFORCE and VS-Code-ribbon halves of flag 13 stand exactly as written — those brands really are absent and really do publish nothing citable. The Microsoft half needs a better test than absence, and Microsoft supplies one itself (flag 26). What it does not change: aspx still ships neutral, because the .NET mark cannot hold 16 px (flag 26) — the sourcing objection dies and the legibility one does not. Worth knowing for later slices: csharp, fsharp and vb also have CC0 artwork in that same repo, and blazor and fsharp are in simple-icons. The Microsoft tail is more sourceable than A01 has assumed.

flags.title: azure and azurestreamanalytics — declined on Microsoft's own published terms
flags.superseded: SUPERSEDED by the fix-round ruling (2026-09-03). This is the cleanest licence decline in the slice — it quotes Microsoft's own terms verbatim — and the ruling voids licence as a gate outright, so it falls without needing the vendored-MIT-copy question it raised to be answered at all. azure ships the Azure "A"; azurestreamanalytics fell back to it on a MEASUREMENT, not a licence. See flag 43. The terms stay recorded verbatim on the subject.
flags.text: With flag 25 removing "absent from simple-icons" as the test, the Azure decline needs to stand on something better, and it does — on terms Microsoft prints itself. Microsoft publishes the Azure marks as the Azure architecture icon set, behind an agreement page that reads, verbatim: "Microsoft permits the use of these icons in architectural diagrams, training materials, or documentation. You can copy, distribute, and display the icons only for the permitted use unless granted explicit permission by Microsoft. Microsoft reserves all other rights." A file-type icon inside a shipped editor is none of those three uses, and R1's pipeline necessarily MODIFIES the artwork — affine fit, gradient flattening — which the terms do not permit at all. That is a decline with a citation rather than an inference. The complication, which is real and is not smoothed over: Azure/bicep is MIT and vendors that entire icon set at src/vscode-bicep-ui/.../azure-architecture-icons/, including analytics/00042-icon-service-Stream-Analytics-Jobs.svg — which is azurestreamanalytics's official artwork, sitting inside an MIT repository. Whether a repo licence can re-license artwork its rights-holder publishes under narrower terms is a question for you and not for a build, so both readings are on the record and neither is assumed. Note that bicep itself does not raise this: its logo is original to that repo, which is why bicep ships and azure does not (flag 28). To overturn: rule that the vendored MIT copy governs, and both icons become their real Azure marks in one edit.

flags.title: Five marks that exist, four cleanly licensed, and none that holds 16 px
flags.superseded: PARTLY SUPERSEDED (fix round, 2026-09-03) — and this is the flag the fix round argued with hardest, because three of its five were second-attempt wins. appscript, aspx and blade all ship now, on reductions this flag said were not available; autohotkey and behat were re-measured and stand. See flags 44, 45 and 46 for the numbers.
flags.text: Tranche 2 had four of these; this tranche has five more, and the pile is now the largest single reason icons go neutral in A01 — ahead of licensing. Every one is rendered at a true 16 px in proofs/sourced-but-illegible-study.png so the verdicts can be checked instead of believed. appscript: Google Apps Script, simple-icons CC0 at Google's own #4285F4 — a fan of five tapering blades plus four dots, nine subpaths, ink runs 0.25–0.88 px at the widest fit the grid allows. Thickening fuses the fan (0.5 px between blades); deleting blades leaves three bars. aspx: the .NET logo, CC0 from Microsoft's own brand repo — a #512BD4 field with the four-glyph ".NET" logotype knocked out, stems 19.2 of 456 source units, 0.54 px at the compact envelope. The study puts it beside abap, whose SAP letters measure 1.00–1.25 px and passed, so the comparison is visible rather than asserted. autohotkey: tranche 2's flag 21 re-measured from this side and confirmed — nothing over 0.50 px, #334455 at 1.86:1, and the study lifts the ink to show colour is not the problem. blade: Laravel's own logomark is a WIREFRAME whose median run is 0.50 px; filling it solid leaves a plain hexagon that is not the mark and would collide with bicep. behat: L2 tier 3, built from vscode-icons' MIT vector of the hand-drawn "B", strokes at 0.50 px, and at 16 px a gray blob with a hole. To overturn any of these you are ruling that an icon may ship illegible, which every version of this guide has refused.

flags.title: bicep ships — the Microsoft counter-example, and why the licence really is different
flags.text: The brief asked whether Azure/bicep's MIT licence actually covers its logo assets. It does, and it was checked rather than assumed. Microsoft's OSS repositories normally attach a trademark notice that carves logos out of the repo licence — the standard "Authorized use of Microsoft trademarks or logos is subject to Microsoft's Trademark & Brand Guidelines" clause. Azure/bicep has no such clause anywhere: not in LICENSE (plain MIT, no rider), not in README, not in CONTRIBUTING, not in SECURITY. docs/images/BicepLogoImage.svg is therefore MIT-licensed artwork, and bicep ships its real mark while azure does not — which is exactly what makes the Azure decline a line rather than a mood. What the rider did. The mark is an isometric cube with a white arm-and-dumbbell figure drawn across it at stroke-width 4 on a 128-unit artboard = 0.40 px, and L8 bans strokes. The reduction redraws nothing: the file already contains a closed, filled path of the same figure (the #1D4A79 silhouette it paints the line work over), so that path ships in the line work's own official white. Same geometry, brand's colour, a weight that reads. What it costs, and the fidelity pane shows it: the official figure is an OUTLINE, so filling it closes the ring at the elbow and the hexagonal nut in the fist — the icon arrives as a cube with a solid white curl on it rather than as an arm lifting a dumbbell. Punching the ring back in was measured and rejected: its official wall is 2 of 128 source units, 0.30 px at this fit. What survives is what L5's detail budget asks to survive — the mark's gestalt, minus its interior detail. What was dropped: the five cube-face polygons, which are alpha-composited shading at opacity 0.7 (L8 bans opacity, and compositing them by hand would invent hexes the file never declares). The cube keeps its silhouette and loses its facetting. Which blue: the field's gradient runs #1D4A79 to #45CAF2 and is flattened to its offset-1 stop, the reading chrome ratified; that stop measures 9.73:1 on the editor ground where the other measures 2.04:1. All of it is in proofs/bicep-reduction-study.png.

flags.title: autohotkey — tranche 2's flag 21 executed, and no family declared
flags.text: Flag 21 deliberately withheld a family declaration for ahk2 and asked this tranche to measure autohotkey itself and reach its own verdict, so that a fiction would not be recorded from one side. Done, independently, and it comes out the same. On the same simple-icons trace at the same compact envelope: nothing in the AutoHotkey keycap exceeds 0.50 px of sustained ink (outline wall and "AHK" letter stems both 0.25–0.50, 25th percentile 0.63), and the official #334455 measures 1.86:1 on the #121314 ground at L 26.7, above the L 22 the lift rule triggers on. proofs/sourced-but-illegible-study.png renders it twice, once in the official ink and once lifted, to show that colour is not the problem. So the pair is now consistently recorded: autohotkey and ahk2 both ship the generic-code glyph, both sit in the merged collapse group, both are byte-identical, and NO family is declared for either — there is no family mark for a base to be identical to, which is precisely what flag 21 predicted. If you overturn the legibility call, ahk2 and autohotkey become a rule-1(b) family and the declaration goes here, in the module where the base lives.

flags.title: bats is a BRANDED icon that will look neutral in the tree
flags.text: Not a decision to make, a consequence to see before you see it in the tree. Bats-core publishes its own mark in its own MIT repo — a bat in flight, and this is a real brand-tier find — and the colours it publishes it in are #B1BBC0 with #FFFFFF wing panels. The set's neutral ink is #A6AEB6. Those are 10 degrees of hue, 4 of lightness and 1 of saturation apart: bats is a branded icon whose official palette lands inside the set's own neutral lane, and the twin audit will pair it with every gray glyph in the S < 25 lane it reports. L6's achromatic exemption forbids clamping a hueless ink — it is the rule that stopped R4 turning editorconfig's white mascot red — so the brand's gray ships and form is what separates it. The second thing to look at: what survives at 16 px is the wing V and the body between its peaks; the four white panels inside the wings (0.38–0.75 px edges against a 2.50 px wing mass) do not resolve, so the icon arrives as a bat SILHOUETTE rather than as the illustrated mark. The verdict is recorded as marginal for both reasons. The repo ships light-mode and dark-mode files as its own two palettes; the dark-mode file is what ships here, which is the reading tranche 2 ratified on alchemy.

flags.title: ballerina — L2's third tier, used a second time and corroborated twice
flags.text: Tranche 2 opened L2's third tier on antlr and then lost the icon to the twin audit, so this is the first subject in the set to actually SHIP from it, and the hunt is on the record in full. Tier 1 exists and is the wrong file: ballerina.io publishes images/ballerina-logo.svg, which is the WORDMARK ONLY — 660×122 units of #464646 letterforms with no symbol anywhere in the file — and its favicon is an .ico. Every plausible symbol URL answers 404. Tier 2 is empty: simple-icons has no ballerina entry. Tier 3 is corroborated: vscode-icons (MIT) and Material (MIT) each carry a vector of the same mirrored dancer-pair symbol, drawn independently and agreeing shape for shape, which is what separates a faithful vector of a real mark from one theme's invention. vscode-icons' ships and is kept at sources-svg/ballerina-vsicons.svg. Colour: vscode-icons paints #20B4AE and Material #00BFA5; brand-colors.json has no ballerina entry so no source-of-truth rule fires, and #20B4AE — the teal ballerina.io itself uses — ships. What this sets up: if tier 3 is acceptable here, the same reasoning would reinstate antlr (flag 18) and would reach appscript, blade and behat — except that those three fail on legibility rather than sourcing, so only antlr actually moves.

flags.title: arduino — the brand's own file is not the brand's own mark
flags.text: A case L2's preference order does not anticipate: the brand tier was reached, the file is genuine, and it is still not what ships. content.arduino.cc publishes Arduino_logo_teal.svg — the infinity over the "Arduino" wordmark, seven paths, all #00878F — and its infinity has three subpaths: the outer contour and two plain loop counters. No plus. No minus. A plain infinity is not the Arduino mark; the minus in the left loop and the plus in the right one are the whole point of the drawing, and simple-icons, Material and vscode-icons all three draw them. So the CC0 trace ships and the brand file stays as the fidelity reference, where you can see the difference for yourself in the provenance pane. What to judge at 16 px: the plus and minus are 1.13 of 24 source units and land on 0.72 px, under L5's floor, and they are kept at official proportions anyway — the docker and chrome reading, where fine official detail is kept rather than thickened. They render as a dark notch in each loop. Thicken them and the loops close up; drop them and the icon is a generic infinity symbol that belongs to nobody.

flags.title: Three brand files, no declared licences — and five that are clean
flags.text: Tranche 1 shipped Google's chrome-logo.svg with "no declared licence" written on the sheet and tranche 2 added four more; the balance improves sharply here, which is worth recording because it is the first tranche where most of the branded subjects are cleanly licensed. No declared terms (the chrome situation): appwrite — appwrite.io's own logomark asset, no terms on the file, though the project itself is BSD-3-Clause. That is the only one of the nine branded subjects in this position. Cleanly licensed: avalonia MIT (AvaloniaUI/Avalonia), avro Apache-2.0 (apache/avro), bats MIT (bats-core/bats-core), bazel Apache-2.0 (bazelbuild/bazel-website), bicep MIT (Azure/bicep, checked for a trademark rider and there is none). Licensed, but by a third party: ballerina is MIT from vscode-icons and the MARK is a WSO2 trademark — the licence covers the vector, not the trademark, which is the same shape of exposure every tier-2 simple-icons subject already carries. CC0 from simple-icons: arduino, autoit. Nothing here needs a decision to proceed; it needs you to know the shape of the exposure and to say if the bar should be higher than chrome set it.

flags.title: Four concepts identified before they were judged — and one trap not walked into
flags.superseded: CARRIED FORWARD, not superseded. Every identification here is still load-bearing and three of them decided a fix-round rebuild: bolt really is FIREBASE Bolt (so Firebase's flame is what applies), blink really is Nuke's BlinkScript (so Nuke's mark was the one built and measured), and the sharkdp/bat trap is still a trap — bat took the terminal object glyph, not that slug.
flags.text: The brief asked for these to be verified rather than assumed, and in four cases the roster label is misleading enough that the verdict would have been wrong without it. atom is not the Atom editor: an .atom file is an Atom FEED (the Atom Syndication Format, RFC 4287), the editor never used the extension, and Material confirms it by mapping .atom to its XML icon alongside .bpmn and .dita. vscode-icons draws a science-diagram atom, which is a pun. bbx is not a BASIC dialect: Material added its bbx icon in the commit "add icons for *.bib files and BibTeX language IDs" and declares it next to cbx and lbx, so it is BibLaTeX's bibliography-style file and belongs with bibliography and bibtex-style. blink is not the browser engine: Material's icon was added as "Added Blink (The Foundry Nuke) icon", so a .blink file is a BlinkScript kernel. bolt is not bolt.new and not Bolt CMS: it is Firebase Bolt, the archived security-rules compiler at FirebaseExtended/bolt. And the trap: simple-icons v16.29.0 carries a slug bat, and it is sharkdp/bat, the Rust cat clone, at #31369E. Shipping it would have put an unrelated brand's mark on every Windows batch file in the tree. It is not used, and this flag exists so nobody uses it later by accident.

flags.title: TOOLING — the slice sheet's stale prose is now driven off the data
flags.text: Tranche 2's flag 22 chartered exactly one file beyond this module, and it is done. tools/build-slice-sheet.mjs had three sentences hard-coded to tranche 1's world and they are now computed from the merged slice and its manifest, with no cosmetic change to a page that is already approved. (1) The coverage sentence said the revision "covers the roster's archive and binary categories"; it now names the categories the built subjects actually carry, taken from the manifest, so it says "archive, binary and code" today and stays right whatever lands next. (2) The prettier-rider count said "one subject needed the prettier rider (onnx)" when three did by tranche 2 and four do now; the sheet counts subjects whose simplification log records a rider and names them, so the number cannot drift again. (3) The "flags 3, 4 and 7 are the ones to argue with" pointer was tranche 1's numbering and had been wrong since tranche 2 landed; the sheet now selects the flags that actually ask for a verdict, reading each flag's own text for the phrases the house style already uses for that ("to overturn", "ruling requested", "your options", "say the word"), with an optional ruling boolean a tranche may set to override the reading. That works on all three tranches without any of them being edited. Two smaller stale spots went with it: the "three came from the brand's own SVG" count and the study filenames named in the footer. Proofs: node tools/gates.mjs A01 and node tools/gates.mjs (pilot mode) both re-run green, and git status shows pilot/ and samples/ byte-clean.

flags.title: THE RULING, and the exact line it moved
flags.text: Recorded first because every flag after it depends on it. Sebastian at the A01 gate, 2026-09-03: "I like the icons that are actually the real Icon. Why is there a lot of the same angled brackets? The licenses don't apply here because this is a personal project and will not be distributed." What that changes: licence, trademark and brand-usage policy NO LONGER GATE SOURCING anywhere in this set. Every subject that went neutral because a mark could not be licensed, or that avoided its true mark on trademark grounds, gets that mark now, and the sourcing chain orders by FIDELITY alone — brand SVG first, then whichever faithful vector of the real mark exists, wherever it is licensed. Repo logos, favicons, product icons and extension assets are all in scope. What it does NOT change, and this is the important half: L5's physics (an icon may still not ship illegible), the prettier-rider and gestalt reading, true colour, the ban on typeset letters, the twin audit, the neutral vocabulary for concepts that genuinely own no mark, and the L2 rule that geometry may never be traced from a raster or drawn freehand — that one is a FIDELITY rule and it still binds, which is why beancount and the Axure app icon are still neutral. Provenance duty is untouched: every source and every licence is still recorded verbatim on this page. We still document what the licence is; it just does not decide. Scale of the change: 20 of the slice's 40 gray-bracket icons leave the collapse, plus vsix and safetensors out of tranche 1's archive and binary glyphs.

flags.title: vsix — the VS Code ribbon ships, and what the mask cost it
flags.text: Flag 3 declined this on three grounds and the ruling voids all three. Sourcing, by fidelity: Microsoft publishes no vector of the mark — the fork's own vscode/resources/ tree holds code.icns and code.ico and no SVG anywhere, and code.visualstudio.com serves PNG — so devicon's MIT trace of the same drawing supplies the geometry. What L8 forced, and what it turned out to cost. The file paints the mark as three tonal wedges (#0065A9 / #007ACC / #1F9CF0) composited through an SVG <mask> whose own path is the official silhouette. L8 bans masks and the pipeline has no boolean intersect, so the wedges cannot be trimmed to that silhouette — but both were built and the difference was MEASURED on a 512 px raster rather than guessed: IoU 0.9910, with 0.28% of the wedges' ink outside the silhouette and 0.62% of the silhouette uncovered. At 16 px that is a fraction of one pixel on the rounded corners. The alternative was the silhouette alone: geometrically exact, and single-tone. R1 keeps multi-colour marks multi-colour, and giving up two of three official tones to buy back 0.3% of area is the wrong trade, so the wedges ship and all three official blues survive. One thing worth recording because it nearly went wrong: the mask path's two subpaths are wound the SAME way, so building it as a single shape under nonzero fill leaves the triangular notch un-punched and the mark comes out as a solid blob with 11% too much ink. The first build of this subject did exactly that and the study caught it; all three renders are in proofs/license-freed-study.png. At 16 px the shipped mark keeps its notch open, the fold between the two darker wedges reads as a fold, and the pale right bar separates.

flags.title: safetensors ships the Hugging Face face — and the MEANING question is still open
flags.text: Flagged for your re-look, because this one is not the same shape as the others. Flag 7 declined the HF face on MEANING and not on licence: safetensors publishes no mark of its own, HF's smiling face is the COMPANY's mark, and .safetensors files are written by dozens of tools with no Hugging Face connection. The ruling settles licence questions; it does not, on its face, settle that one. It is overturned here on your stated preference for the icons that are actually the real icon, plus the fact that Hugging Face created and owns the format (github.com/huggingface/safetensors) — which makes this closer to .pt and PyTorch than the flag allowed. The same reading now carries four more subjects — bolt (Firebase's flame on Firebase Bolt), and, the other way, blink, biml and anyscript stay neutral because their parent marks fail on other grounds. If you would rather a company's mark never stood in for a format it owns, say so and safetensors and bolt go back to their glyphs in one edit. Sourcing: HF's own vector is multi-colour — the #FFD21E face in an #FF9D0B ring, #3A3B45 eyes, an #FF323D mouth, two hands — and simple-icons flattens all of it to one yellow path, so the brand's own file ships and R1 keeps the colours.

flags.title: jar — the licence half of flag 4 is void, and the physics half is not
flags.text: The flag most likely to be argued with, so here is the working. With trademark non-binding the Java cup is sourceable twice over and it was fetched, fitted and measured rather than assumed: the file is kept at sources-svg/java-official.svg and rendered in the provenance pane, and every candidate is at a true 16 px in proofs/license-freed-study.png. The numbers. Oracle's mark is eight tapering brush strokes — four cup rings and two steam swirls, no solid mass anywhere — and at the tall envelope its sustained ink runs are 0.13 px at the 5th percentile, 0.25 at the 25th and 0.38 at the MEDIAN. That is blade's case with worse numbers: not a mark with some thin features, a mark that is nothing but thin features. Three reductions were measured and all three fail: the cup rings without the steam (0.25 px at the 25th percentile); Duke, Java's own mascot, from simple-icons' CC0 openjdk (0.31 / 0.38 px — Duke is a line drawing too); and thickening the rings, which fuses them, their gaps being 0.38–0.69 px apart. The one thing that would work is a redrawn solid cup, and that is freehand geometry for a brand that owns a mark — L2's hard reject, and a FIDELITY rule rather than a licensing one, so the ruling does not reach it. To overturn you would be ruling that this set may draw a brand's mark from memory, which is the ruling that got round 1 thrown out.

flags.title: Six corporate marks reinstated — what each one turned out to be
flags.text: Flag 13 declined six marks on one testable rule and the ruling voids the rule outright. All six ship, and the hunts are worth reading because two of them came out differently from what the flag assumed. al / al-dal — the surprise. Flag 13 said vscode-icons "draws an AL monogram, which R1 has no place for". It is not vscode-icons' monogram: Microsoft draws it. The AL Language extension for Dynamics 365 Business Central (ms-dynamics-smb.al, the extension every .al file is edited with) ships img/AL_file_logo.svg — titled inside the file "AL logo_VS_smallest version_v3" — and registers it in its own file-icon theme against the al language id. vscode-icons is tracing that file, down to the #2EA98E. So this is the brand's own mark for the brand's own file type, and it is a faithful letterform lockup exactly as SAP's "SAP" is: measured, its stems run 1.63–1.81 px, half again thicker than abap's 1.00–1.25 which the gate already passed. al-dal is rule 1(b) on it — Microsoft ships one AL icon for the language, not one per file type. actionscript / adobe-swc. Adobe's corporate red "A", three straight strokes and an open counter, from gilbarbara/logos' faithful vector (Adobe serves no vector from adobe.com under any path that answers). Animate's and Flash Professional's icons were looked at and rejected: both are LETTER PLATES ("An", "Fl"), a monogram in a box, which is what R1's letter ban exists to keep out. adobe-swc is rule 1(b) on actionscript — a .swc is ActionScript compiled. apex. The Salesforce cloud, from devicon's MIT vector, with the "salesforce" wordmark set inside it dropped as a lockup. Flag 13 called this "the painful one, because the cloud would have rendered beautifully"; it does — 1.69 px at the 5th percentile, the most comfortable mark in the tranche. applescript — the one still worth arguing about. AppleScript's OWN icon was hunted first, as its identity really is the Script Editor parchment scroll; that scroll lives inside macOS as .icns raster and Apple publishes no vector of it, and L2 hard-rejects tracing a raster — a FIDELITY rule the ruling does not reach. So the Apple logo ships, lifted to L 88 by the one documented L2 rule (Apple publishes the mark in black and white only). That leaves the company-mark-for-a-language objection standing, the same one flag 38 raises for safetensors; both are yours to rule on together.

flags.title: antlr is REINSTATED — and this is the one to look at before you accept it
flags.text: Look at proofs/antlr-chrome-study.png before reading further. antlr was never a licence decline: it was sourced, built, rendered as the cleanest circle-and-glyph in the slice, and then removed by the cross-set twin audit for colliding with tranche 1's chrome. Flag 18 listed three ways out and the ruling takes the second: "rule that two brands whose real marks genuinely resemble each other may both keep them and relax R8 for declared pairs". What is now in the engine. A new LOOK-ALIKE lane in audit.mjs, chartered by this ruling. A declared pair is reported with its LIVE R7/R8 scores on every run and never fails; the declaration must name both ids and the ruling that opened it, and lives in the tranche that owns the mark. An undeclared pair scoring the same still fails, which is the whole point — this is a lane, not a mute button, and it prints exactly what it is exempting. The numbers have not changed, because the geometry has not: R8 form 0.798 against the 0.72 bar, area IoU 0.969 (two discs of the same diameter are one silhouette), the two dominant reds 3.4 degrees of hue apart. What you are accepting: in the tree a .crx and a .g4 are both a red disc, told apart by a white "A" against four coloured blades. The study renders them side by side at a true 16, 22 and 32 px. If that is a step too far, say so and antlr goes back to the glyph and the lane closes — it has exactly one member and exists only for this pair.

flags.title: The second rider attempts — four marks re-measured with sourcing free, four still out
flags.text: The ruling freed the licences and not the physics, and flag 14's four are where that shows. Every one was rebuilt and re-measured with the whole source pool open, and every reduction that could be attempted was attempted — the bar being the pilot's own editorconfig, which went from "a line drawing cannot survive" to an approved reduction. ada. ada-lang.io's "Ada" logotype, CC0 from simple-icons. At the flat envelope — the widest fit the grid allows — the lockup is 15.2 × 6.5 px and its ink runs measure 0.19 px at the 5th percentile, 0.75 at the 25th, 0.94 at the median. The dotenv reduction has nothing to reduce TO: dropping letters off a three-letter logotype leaves "A", which is a letter and not a mark, and Ada publishes no square mark to fall back on the way npm did. agda. The project's own bird, drawn entirely in 36-unit strokes on a 1200-unit mark = 0.37 px, with an OPEN body contour. Filling it as a silhouette invents the closure and produces a gray blob with two eyes that is not the bird; thickening to L5's floor fuses the three parallel head strokes, which have 0.73 px of clearance. Both are rendered in proofs/agda-and-friends-study.png. ahk2 (with autohotkey). Three reductions measured: the keycap at official weight (nothing over 0.50 px), the keycap with its ink LIFTED out of the #334455 contrast problem (identical legibility — colour was never the binding constraint), and the keycap with its counter shrunk to put the wall on 1.50 px. Only the third clears the floor and only by deleting the "AHK", which leaves a plain rounded-square ring: not the mark, and a shape the vocabulary already spends on generic-binary. apl. Unchanged and not a licence case at all — APL has no owner and no official mark; the APL Wiki's community logo is a matrix-subdivided apple-cube whose defining feature is the subdivision. All four stay on the glyph, and the thing to notice is that the reason is now uniform: every subject still carrying gray brackets in this tranche is there because it cannot be READ, or because there is genuinely nothing to draw.

flags.title: azure ships — and azurestreamanalytics fell back on a measurement, not a licence
flags.text: Flag 26 is the best-argued licence decline in the slice — it quotes Microsoft's own terms verbatim rather than inferring anything — and the ruling voids it outright, which also means the hard question it raised (whether Azure/bicep's MIT licence can re-license artwork Microsoft publishes under narrower terms) never has to be answered. The terms stay written on the subject, verbatim, because provenance duty is untouched. Sourcing, and a finding worth recording: the Azure ARCHITECTURE icon set does not contain the corporate "A" at all. The fix round walked the copy Azure/bicep vendors — 176 files across nineteen categories — and every one is a SERVICE icon; the mark itself is published as no vector by Microsoft anywhere. So the geometry is devicon's MIT vector of the same official artwork, with its two gradients flattened to their offset-1 stops (#0669BC, #2892DF) and the flat #0078D4 connector kept, which is also brand-colors.json's Azure blue. What was dropped: a fourth layer — a shading wash whose five gradient stops declare stop-opacity only (0.3 falling to 0) and no stop-color at all, i.e. black at low alpha: the shadow under the fold. L8 bans opacity and there is no hex to flatten it to, because the file never writes one. That is bicep's cube-face reduction, again. azurestreamanalytics is the interesting half. Its OWN official artwork is now available too, and the fix round built it rather than assuming: 00042-icon-service-Stream-Analytics-Jobs.svg, a gray gradient cog with three cyan stream arcs threaded through it. The arcs are 0.9-unit strokes on an 18-unit artboard and land on 0.65 px; the whole mark measures 0.50 / 0.69 / 1.19 px. Dropping the arcs leaves a cog, which is not the mark and is a generic object besides. So this is the first time working rule 1 branch (a) had a real variant glyph to adapt and LOST it to L5, and the honest fallback is branch (b): .asaql is an Azure service file, so it ships the Azure mark byte-identically. Both are in proofs/license-freed-t3-study.png.

flags.title: aspx ships the .NET plate — and asp is the one family call that is a judgement
flags.text: The reduction first, because it is not a judgement at all. Flag 27 declined the .NET mark saying "the only reductions available are dropping the field (leaving a bare wordmark, which is ada's case) or dropping letters (leaving '.N', which is not a mark)". The pilot had already ruled otherwise: dotenv's official ".ENV" measured 0.50 px, the prettier rider dropped the N and the V, scaled the surviving ".E" 2.5x as ONE group and re-centred it on the square, and the pilot gate approved it as built. The .NET numbers are the same to two decimals: measured on the letters alone, the official ".NET" stems land on 0.50 px, and the surviving ".N" at dotenv's own k = 2.5 comes back at 1.25–1.38 px, over L5's floor. k = 2.2 was measured too and lands on 1.13, under it. Every letterform is Microsoft's own geometry and the pair's spacing is the file's own. The source is the cleanest-licensed in the slice either way: github.com/dotnet/brand, CC0-1.0, which flag 25 found. Now the judgement, and it is genuinely split. The roster gives asp the extensions .asa, .asax, .ascx, .asp AND .aspx, and gives aspx the extensions .ascx and .aspx. They OVERLAP on two, and three of asp's five (.asax, .ascx, .aspx) are ASP.NET files. Converged (what ships): both take the .NET mark as a rule-1(b) family, the tree is consistent, and the cost is that a classic Global.asa wears .NET's mark although classic ASP predates .NET by five years. Split (the alternative): aspx takes the mark and asp stays on the gray glyph, which is more correct about 1996 and means a Global.asax — an ASP.NET file — gets a gray glyph, and which of the two icons a .aspx actually shows then depends on which matcher rule wins. Convergence is what ships and it is one line to split.

flags.title: appscript and blade — two reductions flag 27 said were not available
flags.text: Neither of these was ever a licence case, so the fix round owed them a second attempt at the reduction rather than a re-hunt — the bar being the pilot's own editorconfig, which went from "a line drawing cannot survive" to an approved reduction in one round. appscript. The official mark is nine subpaths: four tapering blades and FIVE detached pivot dots, and at the open envelope it measures 0.75 px at the 5th percentile and 0.94 at the 25th — a blue scatter at 16 px, exactly as flag 27 said. What flag 27 did not try is the reduction L5's detail budget actually asks for: drop the five dots, keep the four blades. That takes the ink to 2.25 px at the 25th percentile and 3.06 at the median, and every blade keeps its official contour, angle and position — nothing thickened, moved or redrawn. What arrives is a blue fan, which is the mark's gestalt; what is lost is studs that never resolved. blade. Flag 27 said "filling it solid leaves a plain hexagon, which is not the mark and would collide with bicep". It is not a plain hexagon: Laravel's logomark is an isometric "L" and its OUTER CONTOUR is that L — stepped and asymmetric, with the notch cut out of its top right. The wireframe seams are the interior detail, the official wireframe's MEDIAN run is 0.44 px, and the contour alone measures 2.00 px at the 5th percentile and 5.19 at the 25th. That is bicep's trade, approved at the pilot gate: the cube lost its facetting and kept its silhouette. What the rider costs is stated on the subject and visible in the fidelity pane: the official mark reads as a wireframe BLOCK and this reads as a flat red L. Keeping the widest single seam was measured (0.50 px) and rejected — one seam of eight reads as a scratch rather than as structure. The bicep collision was CHECKED and not assumed; the twin audit scores the pair on every run and prints the number.

flags.title: The rider attempts that failed — behat, blink and autohotkey, re-measured
flags.text: Recorded at the same length as the wins, because a fix round that only reports its successes is not evidence. behat. Re-measured at 0.44 / 0.94 / 1.25 px for the 5th, 25th and 50th percentiles. The rider has no move available here and that is a structural fact rather than a preference: the tier-3 vector is a SINGLE closed contour tracing a brush stroke — no counters to shrink the apib way, no strokes to widen the alchemy way, no second filled path to adopt the bicep way. Thickening it would need a path offsetter the pipeline does not have, and would be a redraw if it had one. blink. This one changed CATEGORY rather than outcome. Flag 23 filed it under "a product's mark is not the format's", and the fix round overturns that reading for safetensors and bolt — so Nuke's mark had to be built and measured rather than declined on meaning. It fails on L5: the mark is a ring inside a ring with a small rotor glyph, measuring 0.56 / 0.63 / 0.94 px, and at 16 px it is a gray disc with a smudge. It would also land in the antlr/chrome disc neighbourhood, and the fix round has spent its one declared look-alike. autohotkey (with ahk2). Three reductions measured, in flag 42, and the only one that clears the floor does so by deleting the "AHK" and leaving a rounded-square ring. The brand's own modern logo was fetched too and is worse: 137.78 × 22.19 units of "AutoHotkey" spelled out as seventy-five gradient-painted keycaps. All three stay on the glyph, and all three are now legibility verdicts rather than sourcing ones, which is the shape the whole neutral pile has taken.

flags.title: bashly-hook — the mask objection was a reader bug, not a law
flags.text: Flag 23 filed this under "no mark" on the grounds that bashly's symbol is "a hexagonal chevron with a '$' knocked out of it by an SVG mask element — and L8 bans masks, the mask being the entire content of the glyph". L8 bans masks in the shipped icon; it does not ban reading one. The mask here is the simplest kind there is: a white rectangle that shows everything, with the "$" painted black over it to hide that shape. "The chevron except where the $ is" is the definition of a COUNTER, so converting it is the same class of move as tranche 3's own polygon reader on bicep and the engine's circle reader — every coordinate is the file's own, the chevron is emitted clockwise and the $ counter-clockwise, and nonzero winding punches the hole the mask described. Measured at the compact envelope: 1.88 px at the 25th percentile with the $'s counter open at 1.56 px. The wordmark beside the symbol is dropped as a lockup (the apex reading), and the official #434343 — which is drawn for a light README and measures 2.01:1 on the editor ground — is lifted to L 88 by the one documented L2 rule, hue and saturation untouched. The 16 px verdict is MARGINAL and says why: the chevron and the $'s vertical bar hold, the S-curve does not, so what arrives is a light arrow with a slot in it rather than a legible dollar. It ships because it is a real mark and a distinct one; if you would rather have the gray brackets than a marginal symbol, this is the subject to say it on. No family is declared, unchanged from tranche 3: bashly itself is not an A01 roster id, so there is no base here for rule 1 to make this a variant of.

flags.title: The vocabulary opens twice — the stopwatch and the terminal
flags.text: This is a rule change and it is flagged as one. Five concepts left the gray brackets not because a licence fell but because working rule 2's OBJECT branch was read more generously, and that reading will travel. The stopwatch (bench-js, bench-jsx, bench-ts). Flag 24 measured this glyph clean and said so in as many words — 1.38 px minimum, 2.25 at the 25th percentile, R8-clean against the entire vocabulary at under 0.40 on a 0.72 bar, "nothing technical stands in its way" — and declined it on one sentence: "a benchmark names a measurement", not an object. The fix round reads the branch as the object a concept is MEASURED WITH, where that object is unambiguous and universal. A benchmark is timed; the stopwatch is not a metaphor for it the way a lightning bolt is a metaphor for speed. Reading 3 is untouched and still out: painting js's and ts's official hexes onto a stopwatch neither language draws composes a mark no brand publishes, which no licence ruling reaches. The precedent still travels and now travels somewhere specific: every per-language variant family in every later slice — test-js, spec-ts, stories-tsx — lands on ONE shared object glyph in the neutral gray, never the languages' own colours. The terminal (awk, bat). This one needed no rule change at all. Tranche 3 built it, measured it R8-clean, and declined it for exactly one stated reason: "tranche 2 already put applescript on the generic-code glyph, so adding the glyph now would make the set inconsistent with a decision three subjects ago". applescript moved to the Apple logo in this round, so the reason is gone. A .bat and a .awk are run in a terminal, Material independently files both with its shell icon, and cmd.exe's own icon is a PE resource Microsoft publishes as no vector — so the object is the honest icon. Measured 1.81 / 2.63 px, one sub-shape with two counters, nothing that can fuse. What you may want to rule on: whether the terminal should also carry the shell and bash concepts when they arrive, which is a later slice's question but this round's precedent; and whether bashly-hook, whose files are literally src/before.sh, belongs on the terminal rather than on bashly's own symbol. It ships on the symbol, because R1 prefers a real mark.

flags.title: THE BRACKET COUNT — forty is now twenty, and what the twenty are
flags.text: The question that opened the gate was "why is there a lot of the same angled brackets?", and this is the answer in numbers. Forty of eighty-four carried the generic-code glyph; twenty do. Fifteen found real marks once licence stopped gating or once a reduction was attempted a second time — actionscript, adobe-swc, al, al-dal, antlr, apex, applescript, appscript, asp, aspx, azure, azurestreamanalytics, bashly-hook, blade, bolt — and five moved onto the two new object glyphs (awk and bat to the terminal, the three bench ids to the stopwatch). Add vsix and safetensors, which came off tranche 1's archive and binary glyphs, and seventeen subjects gained a real mark in this round. Counting the whole slice rather than one glyph: 84 icons, 54 now carrying a real mark against 37 before, and 30 on the neutral vocabulary against 47. The twenty that remain, sorted by why: (a) the mark exists and cannot be read at 16 px — ada, agda, ahk2, autohotkey, behat, blink. Six, every one re-measured this round with sourcing free, every reduction attempted and logged (flags 42 and 46). (b) there is genuinely no mark to draw — affectscript, anyscript, apl, atom, ats, bak, bbx, befunge, bibliography, bibtex-style, biml, blitzbasic. Twelve, and these are not declines at all: a published IETF format, a POSIX-adjacent esoteric language, a company that no longer exists, a wiki's community logo, a state rather than a thing. (c) the artwork is raster only — axure, beancount. Two, and this is the one class the ruling deliberately does NOT reach: tracing a raster is freehand geometry, which L2 rejects on fidelity, and that is the rule the round-1 rejection created. Nothing in the twenty is there for a licence any more. If you want the number lower still, the remaining levers are: rule that a redrawn mark is acceptable when the official one cannot be read (which would take jar, ada, agda, ahk2, autohotkey, behat and blink, and would reverse the round-1 rejection); or open more object glyphs, one measured R8 check at a time, for the concepts in pile (b) that name something — bak names a copy, atom names a feed.

flags.title: TOOLING — the five engine edits this round made, and their proofs
flags.text: Everything the fix round changed outside the three tranche modules, with the proof for each. (0) color.mjs — the one that is a SET CONSTANT and wants your ruling. The L2 visibility lift triggered on L < 22, which was calibrated on the only case the pilot had (markdown's pure black) and measures the wrong thing: L5's duty is about CONTRAST against the backdrop. L 22 achromatic is #383838, which measures 1.59:1, so the old rule fired only below about 1.6 — which is why tranche 2 had to write "no lift rule reaches it" of AutoHotkey's #334455 at 1.86:1, and why bashly's #434343 at 1.88:1 hit the same gap. The trigger now tests contrast at 3.0:1 (WCAG 2.1's non-text minimum), target unchanged at L 88, hue and saturation still untouched. The set's own evidence brackets that line from both sides: the dimmest branded PRIMARY it has ever shipped is autoit's #5D83AC at 4.70:1, and the dimmest field it REJECTED is bicep's #1D4A79 at 2.04:1 — nothing sits between 2.4 and 4.7. The lift is still OPT-IN per subject, so no icon that does not call it can move: the three callers are markdown, applescript and bashly-hook, and the pilot's 44 files are byte-identical after the change. (1) geom.mjs gains two vocabulary glyphs, terminalGlyph() and stopwatchGlyph(), both shipped unchanged from the drawings tranche 3 already built and measured in its own studies — no existing function was touched, so no existing icon can move. (2) audit.mjs gains the LOOK-ALIKE lane flag 41 charters: a declared pair is reported with its live R7/R8 scores and never fails, an undeclared pair scoring the same still fails, and the lane prints what it is exempting on every run. It is fed from the registry (LOOKALIKE), so a declaration lives in the tranche that owns the mark. (3) build-slice.mjs records the round: a fix_round block in the manifest (the pilot's own pattern) merged from each tranche's FIX_ROUND, and the neutral vocabulary list is now read off the registry instead of being hard-coded — the same staleness bug flag 22 caught on the sheet, fixed in the manifest before it could bite. (4) build-slice-sheet.mjs gains the fix-round strip: every rebuilt subject shown as what-it-was next to what-it-is, at a true 16 px, plus supersession banners on the flags the ruling overturned. Flags are numbered so the gate's own 1–35 keep their numbers and the fix round's continue from 36. Proofs: node tools/gates.mjs A01 green at 84/84 with 0 failures and 0 undeclared collisions; node tools/gates.mjs (pilot mode) green; git status shows pilot/ and samples/ byte-clean; every A01 subject the fix round did NOT touch was sha256-compared before and after and is byte-identical; and the pilot's own 44 files were sha256-compared across the color.mjs edit specifically.

source.name: Bicep (brand's own SVG)
source.note: 128x128, ten layers: a gradient-filled outer hexagon (a `polygon` element), five cube faces at opacity 0.7, a solid #1D4A79 silhouette of the arm-and-dumbbell figure, four white shapes at opacity 0.2-0.3 and a white line drawing of the figure at stroke-width 4. Azure/bicep is plain MIT with NO trademark or logo clause anywhere in its LICENSE, README, CONTRIBUTING or SECURITY files — checked, because that is what separates this from azure. Fetched to sources-svg/bicep-official.svg

simplifications: the outer hexagon is a `polygon` element and is re-emitted as a closed path from its own `points` attribute — a format conversion in which every coordinate is the file's own, not a transcription of the kind tranche 2 declined for SAP's polyline

the field's gradient (#1D4A79 at offset 0, #45CAF2 at offset 1) is flattened to its offset-1 stop, the reading chrome ratified. That stop measures 9.73:1 on the #121314 ground; the offset-0 stop measures 2.04:1 and would half-sink the field into the backdrop. Both are rendered in proofs/bicep-reduction-study.png

the five cube-face polygons are DROPPED: they are alpha-composited shading at opacity 0.7 over the gradient, L8 bans opacity, and compositing them by hand would invent hexes the file never declares. What is lost is the cube's facetting; what is kept is its silhouette, which is what reads at 16 px

PRETTIER RIDER, without redrawing anything: the mark's figure is a white LINE DRAWING at stroke-width 4 on a 128-unit mark, i.e. 0.40 px, and L8 bans strokes. The file already contains a closed FILLED path of the same figure (the #1D4A79 silhouette it draws the line work over), so that path ships painted in the line work's own official #FFFFFF — the brand's geometry, in the brand's colour, at a weight that reads. After the rider the thinnest sustained run in the icon is 2.50 px

WHAT THE RIDER COSTS, stated because the fidelity pane shows it: the official figure is an OUTLINE, so filling it closes the ring at the elbow and the hexagonal nut in the fist, and the figure arrives as one solid white curl rather than as an arm lifting a dumbbell. Punching the ring back in was measured and rejected — its official wall is 2 of 128 source units, which is 0.30 px at this fit. What survives is the gestalt L5's detail budget asks for: the cube, and a curled arm on it

proof_16px.note: reads as the cube plus the curled-arm figure, which is the mark's gestalt, and nothing in it is under 2.50 px. Be clear about what the rider COST, because the fidelity pane shows it: filling the official line drawing solid closes the ring at the elbow and the hex nut in the fist, so the figure arrives as one white curl rather than as an arm lifting a dumbbell. lookalike_lane.ruling: Sebastian, 2026-09-03 — "I like the icons that are actually the real Icon." Flag 18 offered exactly this as its second option: relax R8 for DECLARED pairs rather than take a real mark off a real brand.
lookalike_lane.why: ANTLR's mark is an orange-red disc with a white "A" and Chrome's is a red-yellow-green disc with a blue centre. They score R8 form 0.798 on a 0.72 bar (area IoU 0.969: two discs of the same diameter are one silhouette) and their dominant reds are 3.4 degrees of hue apart. Both are the brands' own artwork, neither can be refitted out of the collision — the envelope law has no room to shrink one disc by a quarter — and the alternative is a gray glyph on one of them. Rendered side by side at a true 16 / 22 / 32 px in proofs/antlr-chrome-study.png.

twin_audit.note: CROSS-SET: the pilot's 20 subjects and every subject this slice built are scored in one pool. THREE lanes are exempt from R8 and reported rather than failed, because in all three the identity is declared and deliberate — FAMILY (working rule 1), NEUTRAL COLLAPSE (working rule 2) and LOOK-ALIKE (opened by the A01 fix round, 2026-09-03: two brands whose real marks genuinely resemble each other may both keep them, and the pair is reported with its live scores every run). An undeclared pair scoring the same still fails. PLATE marks are scored glyph-to-glyph against m11's BADGE bar of 0.92.
